column1: For scores 95,95,88,88,88,70 ordered descending, what do row_number(), rank(), and dense_rank() output?
column2: row_number: 1,2,3,4,5,6 (always unique). rank: 1,1,3,3,3,6 (ties share, then skip the used-up positions). dense_rank: 1,1,2,2,2,3 (ties share, no gaps).

column1: Which SQL ranking function gives tied rows the same number with NO gap afterward, and what's the verbal rule?
column2: dense_rank(). It numbers the distinct values: "how many distinct values are above me, plus one." (rank() would skip; row_number() never ties.)

column1: How does rank() differ from dense_rank() on ties?
column2: Both give tied rows the same number, but rank() then SKIPS the used-up positions (1,1,3), while dense_rank() leaves no gap (1,1,2). rank() = "how many rows strictly ahead of me, plus one."

column1: Why should you never rely on row_number() to break ties without an explicit tiebreaker?
column2: Among tied rows the order is arbitrary and can change between runs — the engine numbers them in whatever internal order it has. Add a real tiebreaker to ORDER BY (e.g. ORDER BY score DESC, id).

column1: How do you write LAG/LEAD in ClickHouse, and what is the frame gotcha?
column2: ClickHouse has no LAG/LEAD; use lagInFrame(x, offset, default) / leadInFrame(...). They obey the window frame, whose default (with ORDER BY) ends at CURRENT ROW — so leadInFrame sees nothing unless you widen it, e.g. ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. lagInFrame works with the default frame.

column1: What does the QUALIFY clause do in ClickHouse?
column2: It filters rows on a window-function result without a wrapping subquery, e.g. ... QUALIFY row_number() OVER (...) = 1. It is to window functions what HAVING is to aggregates.

column1: Difference between LIMIT 10 and QUALIFY dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY x DESC) <= 10?
column2: LIMIT 10 returns exactly 10 rows. QUALIFY dense_rank() <= 10 returns every row in the top 10 ranks, which can be MORE than 10 rows if there are ties. LIMIT cuts rows; QUALIFY-on-rank cuts ranks.

column1: How do ClickHouse CTEs (WITH ... AS) differ from Postgres CTEs in evaluation?
column2: ClickHouse inlines/substitutes a CTE at each reference (re-evaluated every use) instead of materializing it once, so referencing a heavy CTE twice runs it twice. Recursive CTEs exist since v23.4.

column1: What does argMax(a, b) return, and which window function does it replace?
column2: The value of column a at the row where b is maximal (argMin = at the minimum). It is the idiomatic ClickHouse shortcut for first_value/last_value-style "the X at the max/min of Y" without a window.

column1: To get one row per group with its total, use sum() OVER (PARTITION BY g) or GROUP BY g?
column2: GROUP BY g. A window function (sum() OVER) keeps every input row and just annotates each with the group's total — it never collapses to one row per group.

column1: In ClickHouse, can an aggregate go directly inside a window's ORDER BY after GROUP BY?
column2: Yes. e.g. SELECT customer_id, sum(amount), dense_rank() OVER (ORDER BY sum(amount) DESC) FROM t GROUP BY customer_id. Window functions run after aggregation, so the aggregate is available to the window — no subquery needed.

column1: What is the default window frame when a window has ORDER BY but no explicit frame?
column2: RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. This is why sum() OVER (ORDER BY d) is a running total (not the grand total) and why leadInFrame can't see following rows by default.

column1: What happens if you run CREATE TABLE ... IF NOT EXISTS for a table that already exists with a different engine/schema?
column2: Nothing — it is a no-op on existence. Your new engine/columns are silently ignored and the old definition stays. It is idempotent on existence, not on definition; manage schema changes with migrations, not by hoping the DDL matches.

column1: Why does stopping the minikube node's Docker container directly break kubectl/DBeaver, and how do you recover?
column2: It is not a graceful shutdown: the control plane (kubelet/apiserver) stays down and the apiserver returns on a new host port, stale-ing kubeconfig ("connection refused"). Fix: minikube start -p <profile> (rewrites kubeconfig, restarts pods, keeps data). Host port-forwards always die on any stop/restart — re-run them afterward.
